Recursive Self-Improvement

Oriol Vinyals’ framing from his Agentic AI Summit talk.

Self-improvement (SI): a system given a spec runs mostly without user input for hours or days, optimizing toward a fitness function. Autonomous Research Agents includes two instances of this shape: Chuan Li’s Tetris system (“the Lab”), which Vinyals names directly as his own example, and The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt, which governs a long theorem-proving search. Both optimize an external target.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI): the further step where the agent harness’s own code and the model weights themselves become things the system can modify — distinguish harness-level self-improvement (compaction, tool access, orchestration code) from model-level (retraining, fine-tuning from scratch). “The recursivity part is anything that modifies that object.” Plenty of SI has been demonstrated; genuinely impactful RSI hasn’t yet, per Vinyals, though it’s coming.

A more rigorous, two-condition definition, from Ian Fischer’s talk (Poetiq): RSI requires recursive (each step’s improvements drive the next round — it compounds) and self (the system improves itself, not some other target) together, as a strict pair. Fischer’s pointed claim: common usage of “RSI” is simultaneously too permissive — plain iterative-improvement loops get labeled RSI without genuine recursion or self-targeting — and too restrictive — some commentators only count it if you’re updating an LLM’s actual weights, which excludes plenty of other system components that can be effectively improved too.

A cost-vs-genuineness landscape, splitting LLM-centric from systems-oriented approaches: LLM-centric RSI (the best-funded frontier labs) is genuinely RSI but expensive, because it requires training an LLM from scratch at every step. Systems-oriented RSI (Fischer’s own company, plus peers like Darwin Gödel Machines and Sakana) treats the LLM as just one component of a broader system — cheaper, because each RSI step costs only an inference run rather than a training run, and it opens improvement avenues an LLM-only view misses entirely. See Self-Optimizing Optimizers for the specific mechanism Poetiq uses to do this.

Two common “almost-RSI” patterns, each one specific change away from genuine RSI:

  • “AI that builds itself” (Anthropic’s own framing — a version of Claude, inside Claude Code, improved by humans plus Claude Code): only partial RSI, because humans are still in the loop. Anthropic itself doesn’t count it as full RSI while humans remain involved.
  • “Automated AI scientist” (hypothesize → implement → measure → write up → feed back into a knowledge store): typically not RSI at all, per Fischer — the loop targets external tasks, not a piece of the system doing the looping. It only becomes genuine RSI if the loop is specifically pointed at improving the LLM that runs it, which costs far more than a typical setup. This sharpens exactly where Autonomous Research Agents sits: Chuan Li’s Tetris/Lab loop, the Crouzeix proof-search run, and James Zou’s paper-agents pattern all have this “automated AI scientist” shape. By Fischer’s stricter test, none is RSI — all are SI, full stop, unless the loop is retargeted at itself.

The clean bridge from auto-research to RSI is therefore a target switch plus compounding. Point the same ideate → execute → evaluate → retain loop at the agent’s model, harness, prompts, tools, or optimizer; then require the resulting improvement to make the next research cycle better. A system merely learning more about mathematics is doing research. A system whose mathematical research improves the researcher, which then improves its ability to conduct the next round, has the recursive shape.

A four-stage loop, modeled on how human researchers actually work: ideation (which ideas are worth pursuing) → implementation → experimentation (run, debug, iterate or abandon) → evaluation (did the hypothesis hold) → loop. Today’s automation clusters almost entirely in the middle two boxes — coding agents are good at implementation and experimentation — while ideation and evaluation are comparatively untouched and much harder. Vinyals’ claim: these two, not compute, are what actually gate RSI.

Three tiers for evaluating progress toward RSI, increasing in fidelity and cost:

  1. Indirect — hill-climb existing benchmarks and hope RSI emerges as a byproduct. Cheap and well-understood, but an indirect measure prone to overfitting.
  2. Direct/meta — run an agent trying to improve a target metric across repeated attempts and measure the improvement rate itself. Measures the right thing but is expensive and still narrow relative to the real target (“automate my whole frontier lab”).
  3. Process-quality — grade how the improvement happened (creativity, no cheating) against fuzzy criteria like research taste, novelty, elegance — the same criteria a human peer reviewer applies. Ideation specifically is badly underexplored; even human peer review is bad at it (his example: the distillation paper was rejected on first submission).

Why RSI might arrive slower than the hype implies: evaluation and ideation are hard bottlenecks independent of compute; physical constraints don’t disappear (chip speed limits, speed of light); and performance in some domains may already be near an asymptote — more capability doesn’t guarantee “better” once you’re there (his example: models can already write “too well” for some use cases).

A mechanistic reason for the ideation/evaluation bottleneck: Long-Horizon Agents argues RL training’s economics decay quadratically with trajectory length, because a single end-of-trajectory reward gives almost no per-step credit assignment over long horizons. Ideation and evaluation are exactly the kind of long-horizon, hard-to-decompose work this predicts should be hardest to train — which lines up with Vinyals’ observation that those two stages, not compute, are what’s lagging.

A stronger, more specific version of model-level self-improvement: Weizhu Chen predicts in Continuous Model Improvement that models will become able not just to modify themselves but to modify other models — cross-model, not just self-directed. This is a sharper claim than Vinyals’ own model-weight-level self-improvement, which is scoped to a model changing its own weights.

A concrete, real-world instance of the evaluation bottleneck: Mengdi Wang’s talk, Verification as Science’s Bottleneck, shows this playing out at scale, right now, in physical science — AI has sped up hypothesis generation but not verification, to the point that a colleague of hers concludes “science is not faster, science is actually getting slower.”

A possible counterexample to “impactful RSI hasn’t happened yet”: Richard Socher’s talk, Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery, describes a genuinely self-targeted RSI loop — his system applied to improving AI research itself, not an external domain — that beat years of prior human research on three AI-research benchmarks (nanochat, a nanoGPT speedrun, an NVIDIA kernel benchmark) within two days on the first, producing real inventions rather than hyperparameter tuning. Socher frames science/research as three steps — ideation, implementation, validation — and names validation as the still-unsolved bottleneck, echoing Vinyals’ own framing almost exactly.

A concrete methodology for testing whether “recursive” actually holds: RELAI (Sel Fez, Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary startup spotlight) built a continual-learning version of Terminal-Bench, run in two phases, specifically to check whether an agent-optimization method compounds across rounds rather than improving once and plateauing (or worse, showing negative transfer between rounds). Competing methods they tested showed little continuous improvement or active negative transfer between phases; their own regression-controlled optimizer — built from replayable learning environments generated from real production failure signal, not benchmarks alone — showed genuine compounding gains. This is a real answer to a question the definitions above only state abstractly: not just “recursive means each step drives the next,” but a concrete two-phase test for whether a given optimization method actually has that property or is masquerading as it.

Where it shows up

  • Self-Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement — the talk this framing comes from.
  • Autonomous Research Agents — Li’s Tetris/Lab system and the Crouzeix proof-search run show the external-target research loop; by Fischer’s stricter test, both are SI, not RSI.
  • Agent Harness — his harness-vs-model-weights split gives Chen’s “models might build their own harnesses” question a rigorous name and place.
  • Long-Horizon Agents — a mechanistic, economics-based explanation for why ideation and evaluation specifically are the hard stages.
  • Continuous Model Improvement — Chen’s sharper, cross-model version of self-improvement.
  • Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — the same evaluation-bottleneck claim, playing out concretely in physical science.
  • Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — a fourth voice on the ideation/validation bottleneck, plus a concrete self-targeted RSI result that may update the “hasn’t happened yet” claim above.
  • End-to-End AI Research — the same evaluation/ideation-bottleneck claim, playing out concretely in security research, with a striking idea-generation funnel (3,000+ ideas → 4 published results) as evidence.
  • Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck — a sharp, self-referential instance of the same bottleneck: automating algorithm discovery is itself blocked by the sparse-reward problem it’s meant to solve, since current agents aren’t good at discovering genuinely novel algorithms.
  • An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement — Fischer’s more rigorous two-condition definition, taxonomy, and the two almost-RSI patterns.
  • Self-Optimizing Optimizers — Poetiq’s concrete mechanism for cheap, systems-oriented RSI.
  • Paper Agents — another “automated AI scientist”-shaped loop that’s SI, not RSI, by Fischer’s test, since it doesn’t target itself.
  • Architect Agents — harness-level self-improvement one level up: the skill of building harnesses compounding, rather than one harness instance improving itself.
  • Three-Level Runtime Control — sharpens the harness-vs-model-weights split into three specific levels: token steering, action control, and workflow control.
